data.title: Assessing the influence of repeated exposures and mental stress on human wayfinding performance in indoor environments using virtual reality technology

findings.antecedent: virtual fire emergency (visual fire and smoke, auditory fire alarm) during egress task (first exposure)
findings.consequent: travel time (seconds) to complete egress task
findings.mechanism: Fire and smoke reduced environmental visibility, impacting recognition of landmarks and position, and mental stress caused by the emergency affected environmental perception and decision-making, leading to decreased wayfinding performance.

mechanism_chain.to_construct: impaired landmark recognition and position assessment

theory_commitments.specific_claim: environmental stressors can impair the retrieval and use of spatial knowledge from cognitive maps

mechanism_chain.to_construct: impaired landmark recognition and position assessment

theory_commitments.specific_claim: environmental stressors can impair the retrieval and use of spatial knowledge from cognitive maps

findings.antecedent: repeated exposure to the same virtual environment (two weeks apart, normal condition) for treasure hunting task
findings.consequent: travel time (seconds) to complete treasure hunting task

The threshold of repeated exposures for wayfinding performance improvement might vary depending on the environment and individual differences.

limitations: Sample limited to university students, potentially affecting generalization to other age groups or populations.
Study conducted in a virtual reality environment, which may not fully generalize to real-world wayfinding behaviors.
Specific time interval (two weeks) between repeated exposures may influence results, and different intervals require further investigation.
The degree of reality in the IVE could be further enhanced by including additional human senses and dynamic scenarios (e.g., real walking, smell of fire, dynamic obstacles, human group interaction).
